title: Curriculum based course timetabling: new solutions to Udine benchmark instances
contribution: A two-stage IP decomposition (period assignment with Hall's conditions, then per-period bipartite matching for rooms) that solves all four Udine instances to proven optimality for the first time and gives competitive ITC2007 solutions with lower bounds.
problem_entry: Entered through public benchmarks (Udine, ITC2007); closes the open test4 to optimality, conceding instances became easy for modern solvers (pp. 2, 10).
key_idea: Project out the room dimension: stage 1 assigns lectures to periods under Hall's condition, stage 2 is a polynomial min-weight bipartite matching; exact for hard constraints, RS soft constraint costs global optimality (pp. 2-6).
assumptions: Binary IP with exponential Hall inequalities generated as needed; Udine, 14 ITC2007, 7 DDS and 3 simulated TU Berlin instances; exactness for hard constraints only, RS quality loss asserted not measured (pp. 3-4, 11-17).
proof_devices: Hall's marriage theorem as correctness device (p. 3)
solver-attribution reruns with CPLEX 9, SCIP, CBC (pp. 10-11)
ablation by constraint class: dropping CC collapses times (Table 1, p. 10)
experiments: 3.4 GHz PC, CPLEX 11.0.1; CPU time units for budget parity with randomized competitors; solutions validated; borrowed competitor numbers; wins over winner's best on 8/13, over best finalist on 6/13; extensions leave 70-99% gaps (pp. 9-15).
positioning: Continues the IP line in timetabling against the heuristic mainstream; Burke et al.'s branch-and-cut not yet suited for feasible solutions (pp. 2, 13, 15).
writing: Two registers: abstract 'not an overall winner', intro 'often beat'; reader's guide to decisive tables; limitations stated where they arise (pp. 1-2, 10, 15).
limits_future: RS costs optimality, CC hurts times, commercial-solver dependence, no three-index baseline run; future: exploit soft-constraint structure, stable warm-started timetables (pp. 4-17).

method_links.note: Decomposition justified against the three-index model but no compact-model baseline run; projection later called Benders (S048 p. 2); tailored-algorithm belief not measured.

Competitors' numbers borrowed and normalised by CPU units, not rerun; step 6 mixed: 'not an overall winner' vs 'often beat' with 6 of 13 wins.

transferable: Project out a dimension through a combinatorial feasibility theorem (Hall's condition) so that the second stage becomes polynomial; generate only the inequalities actually needed (pp. 3, 15).

Against randomized competitors, give a deterministic method the competitor's total budget across seeds, in a named unit, and print both the competitor's average and its best run (pp. 10-11).
When real data are incomplete, publish a simulator-built instance set "with near real-world character" (p. 15).
Add a one-line reader's guide to the decisive tables (p. 10).

quotes.text: Our algorithm is not an overall winner, but it is very robust in the sense that it deterministically gives satisfactory lower and upper bounds in reasonable computation time without particular tuning.
Since in contrast our approach is entirely deterministic, it is fair to allow ourselves a solution time equivalent to what is used in total in the respective runs of these various groups.

title: Automatic Dantzig-Wolfe Reformulation of Mixed Integer Programs
contribution: An experimental proof of concept that general MIPs can be forced into arrowhead form by hypergraph partitioning and automatically Dantzig-Wolfe reformulated, with relative border area as selection proxy, giving root bounds competitive with CPLEX on average.
problem_entry: Tests the consensus that DWR needs tailoring, against the success of automatic generic cuts; promises only a computational proof of concept (pp. 1-2, 4).
key_idea: Any matrix can be forced into arrowhead form via min-weight balanced hypergraph partitioning; keep original variables in the master; choose among candidates by relative border area (pp. 5-8, 16).
assumptions: General MIP; bound gain from partial convexification; 39 MIPLIB 2003/2010 instances filtered by density, size, integrality, known-structure excluded; ~1500 decompositions; equivalence of remaining B&P/B&C machinery assumed, untested (pp. 4, 8-12, 24).
proof_devices: degenerate-extreme argument rules out dual bound as quality measure (p. 20)
two extremes bracket the time trend: all-border LP vs border-free MIP (p. 17)
DWR auto vs DWR best comparison (p. 22)
du Merle dual stabilisation with documented constants (p. 10)
experiments: Single-thread i7-870, 1 h, root only; gap closed and per-instance z-scored times with LOESS; CPLEX 12.2 root baseline and time-to-same-bound; DWR auto beats CPLEX root on 12/23 and 8/16, best on 16/23 and 10/16; variability across decompositions only, seed fixed at 1 (pp. 10-30).
positioning: Joins matrix re-ordering from numerical linear algebra with generic DWR frameworks that require user-given structure: 'we provide the missing link' (pp. 2-4, 27).
writing: Hedged frame ('proof-of-concept'), Expectation/Observation pairing with flagged mismatches, but headline words ('consistently', 'globally better') outrun counts; artifact warning (pp. 1-3, 16, 21, 27).
limits_future: Root node only, detection one of many approaches, proxy leaves balance/density open, a priori measure out of reach; future: decide a priori whether decomposition pays (S009) (pp. 27-28).

method_links.note: Option space (hypergraph type, weights, k) written down and sampled on real MIPLIB instances; map read for surprises; one proxy kept from six measures.
Steps 1-3: instances where decomposition is not first choice, stated filters, CPLEX rerun on same machine and limit.
Step 6: 'consistently', 'globally better' on 3 of 39, and 16/11 count of DWR best written as 'our DWR approach'; no seed protocol.
Original variables kept in master (step 6); CPLEX defaults as yardstick (step 2); stop rule as integrality filter.

coauthors: Martin Bergner, Alberto Caprara, Alberto Ceselli, Fabio Furini, Enrico Malaguti, Emiliano Traversi

quotes.text: We did not experiment on instances with known structure: in these cases the effectiveness of DWR has already been proven, and indeed, the purpose of our study is to prove that DWR can work for general MIPs.
Of course, at the moment, our work is not intended to produce a competitive tool, but to demonstrate that the direction is promising.

title: Comments on: An Overview of Curriculum-Based Course Timetabling
contribution: A sole-authored discussion that praises the overview and sets an agenda: practice-near definitions, objectives beyond penalty sums, robustness, identical-conditions comparisons and a new ITC.
problem_entry: Asks whether the field needs another overview and answers yes, requesting more advice for practitioners (p. 1).
key_idea: Four critiques (ITC definition far from reality, weighted penalties obscure evaluation, cross-paper comparisons need identical conditions, ask for vision) and a call for a new ITC (pp. 1-3).
assumptions: CB-CTT as standardised by ITC; modelling an extension is not the same as handling it computationally (p. 3).
positioning: Praises overview and ITC fairness; reclassifies his two-stage approach as Benders; discloses bias toward column generation (pp. 1-3).
writing: First-person short sections with wishes, rhetorical questions, bias disclosure, closing exclamation; 'advise' for 'advice' twice (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: Agenda only, no data; no positive alternative to penalty objectives beyond robustness; rerun of old code with fresh CPLEX announced, outcome unknown (pp. 2-3).

method_links.note: Identical conditions, 'grain of salt', bias disclosure; his own 2010 comparison was of the borrowed-numbers kind (inference).
Planned rerun of old decomposition code with fresh CPLEX, not a compact model; repeats tailored-algorithm belief.
As discussant asks for a personal account of suitability and clearer perspectives: survey-as-agenda from the reader's side.

title: An adaptive discretization MINLP algorithm for optimal synthesis of decentralized energy supply systems
contribution: A problem-tailored primal method for nonconvex DESS synthesis (discretised MILP, fix design, repair by per-load-case NLPs, adaptive grid refinement) plus a public instance set, finding feasible solutions on all 320 instances.
problem_entry: Application-driven: simultaneous structure, sizing and operation; metaheuristics give no optimality measure, linearised MILP designs infeasible on 273/320, BARON hits limits (pp. 2-4, 8, 19).
key_idea: Approximate, fix, repair, refine: discretised sizes and piecewise-linear operation give a MILP; fix discrete decisions; repair with BARON NLPs per load case; contract or shift the grid and warm-start (pp. 8-15).
assumptions: Nonconvex MINLP with bilinear terms and nonconvex costs; DESSLib 320 instances in 32 categories via Latin hypercube ±5%; part-load independent of size; repair feasibility not guaranteed (pp. 4-16, 26).
proof_devices: odd k_max keeps chosen size a grid point after contraction (p. 13)
shifted grid respects initial size bounds (p. 13)
experiments: One core i7-3770; BARON 1 h and Voll MILP plus repair, all rerun; primal gap and shifted geometric means; feasible on 320 vs BARON's 202, up to 40% better, fraction of an hour; no dual bounds, one MINLP solver, no variability runs (pp. 16-20).
positioning: Process systems engineering synthesis literature and MINLP discretisation / piecewise-linear methods; coauthors' Voll et al. 2013 MILP as benchmark (pp. 3-4, 7-8).
writing: Abstract broader than results ('solvers' = one solver, 'slightly better'); anomaly flagged 'Irritatingly'; missing bounds admitted; preprint placeholder and typos (pp. 1-2, 18-21).
limits_future: No optimality guarantee, repair not guaranteed, BARON bounds weak; future: dual bounds, superstructure expansion, other synthesis problems (pp. 12, 18, 21).

method_links.note: Steps 3 and 5: every competitor rerun on one core with 1 h limit; shifted geometric means with shifts; solved counts per category.
Step 6: abstract claims more than results text; 'solvers' means one solver.
MINLP setting: BARON on the original model is the yardstick; tailored method justified by its measured failure, not a decomposition probe.

title: Learning When to Use a Decomposition
contribution: A learned gate and selector on top of GCG that decides whether to use a Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition or fall back to SCIP and which decomposition to use, with a labelled dataset of runs; preliminary.
problem_entry: Entered through the failure mode of the group's own tool: GCG beats SCIP only on a small fraction; recast as a yes/no question against SCIP under a time limit (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Classifier (1) gates GCG vs SCIP exit by max predicted probability >= alpha; classifier (2) picks the decomposition; distance-based classifiers under the hypothesis similar decompositions work on similar models (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: General MIP and arrowhead re-arrangement; 300 structured instances in 12 families plus 100 random MIPLIB 2010; 1,619 decompositions; structured label kept out of features (pp. 3-5).
experiments: i7-2600, 2 h limit; one random 3/5 split, 131 test instances (not reconciled with 160); unsolved SCIP 52, GCG 66, SL 44, OPT 39; geo means 127.1/370.4/78.6/67.8 s; no repeated splits, seeds or held-out families (pp. 5-7).
positioning: Builds on S015 and Wang-Ralphs detection and ML in MIP (Hydra-MIP, learning to branch); not aware of learning MIP structure for decompositions (p. 2).
writing: Hedged throughout; candid on tool weakness; 'significant' without a test; precision ~2/3 used to explain 2/3 of potential (recall ~58%) (pp. 1-2, 6-8).
limits_future: Small test set, weak classifier (2), costly detection, feature dependence; future: redesigned detection loop, prediction before detection, strong detection features (pp. 6-8).

method_links.note: Stop rule ('may completely fail'), fallback to branch-and-cut solver, good decomposition = well-solvable pricing; strong detection automates step 4 probe.

quotes.text: GCG, presented with an arbitrary MIP, successfully detects a decomposition that leads to an improved performance over SCIP on the original model only in a small fraction of cases.

As GCG may perform very poorly when not a “right” structure is detected we try to keep the false positives low, even if this implies accepting more false negatives and thus not exploiting the full potential of GCG.
